result.title: A six-month periodic fasting reduces microalbuminuria and improves metabolic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy: a randomized controlled study

knowledge_units.context_summary: A randomized controlled study evaluated the impact of a six-month fasting-mimicking diet on metabolic markers and albuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy. The intervention group showed significant improvements in microalbuminuria and insulin resistance compared to a Mediterranean diet control group. These benefits were partially sustained at follow-up, while markers for DNA damage and dicarbonyl detoxification remained unchanged.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study used a stratified random sampling method, based on Body Mass Index (BMI) and HbA1c levels, to assign patients to either a fasting-like diet (FMD) or a control group that followed a Mediterranean diet (M-diet). The FMD involved specific restrictions on calorie and macronutrient intake for five days of the month, while the M-diet involved a normal calorie intake. Primary and secondary endpoints focused on changes in albumin-to-creatinine ratio, metabolic markers, and safety outcomes, with statistical analysis performed on the intention-to-treat population.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study reports that a six-month Fasting-Mimicking Diet (FMD) significantly reduced microalbuminuria and improved metabolic markers like HOMA-IR and urea levels in type 2 diabetes patients compared to a Mediterranean diet control. While FMD induced greater weight loss, body composition changes were not significantly different between groups, and most metabolic improvements were not sustained at follow-up. The intervention was well-tolerated with only mild to moderate adverse effects reported.

The study reports that hypoglycemic episodes and subjective health status did not differ between the FMD and M-Diet groups, while FMD participants required less antihyperglycemic and antihypertensive medication. Blood ketones increased significantly in the FMD group, and the diet reduced albuminuria specifically in patients with microalbuminuria, an effect comparable to SGLT-2 inhibitors but absent in those with macroalbuminuria. The discussion attributes these effects to shifts in fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis, noting that metabolic improvements were largely reversed after refeeding.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study concludes that while FMD reduced microalbuminuria and improved metabolic markers, it did not activate specific defense pathways for nephropathy reversal, suggesting longer intervention periods may be required. Limitations include the caloric restriction in the FMD group compared to the isocaloric control, though statistical adjustments were made for weight loss. The authors point out that the lack of kidney biopsies has made it difficult to study the metabolism of kidney cells, and that the small sample size necessitates larger studies in the future.
